decks.title: Carboxylic Acids — Part 1: Structure, preparation and acidity
goals: Classify and name mono- and dicarboxylic acids and describe the carboxyl group
Explain high boiling points using hydrogen-bonded dimers
Write equations to prepare aliphatic and aromatic acids from alcohols, aldehydes, nitriles and Grignard reagents
Arrange acids in order of strength using inductive and resonance effects

slides.heading: Carboxylic acids
slides.body_md: Part 1 — compounds with the –COOH group: names, structure, preparation and acid strength.

visual.alt: Table of familiar carboxylic acids

slides.narration: Namaste! The sting of an ant, the sourness of vinegar and the smell of rancid butter all come from carboxylic acids, compounds containing the carboxyl group, COOH. In this part we classify and name them, see why they boil so high, learn how to make them, and find out what makes some acids much stronger than others.

slides.heading: Classification and nomenclature
slides.body_md: **Monocarboxylic** (CₙH₂ₙ₊₁COOH) and **dicarboxylic** acids; aliphatic and aromatic. IUPAC: replace -e by **-oic acid** (C of COOH = C-1); diacids: **-dioic acid**.

visual.alt: Table of names of carboxylic acids

slides.narration: Monocarboxylic acids have one carboxyl group; dicarboxylic acids have two. The IUPAC name replaces the final e of the alkane with oic acid, numbering from the carboxyl carbon: two-methylpropanoic acid. Diacids end in dioic acid: oxalic acid is ethanedioic acid and adipic acid, used for nylon, is hexanedioic acid. Many common names come from natural sources: formic from ants, butyric from butter.

slides.heading: Structure and physical properties
slides.body_md: The carboxyl carbon is **sp²**; the –OH lone pair is delocalised into C=O, so the C=O is less reactive than in aldehydes. Acids form **hydrogen-bonded dimers** (even in the vapour), so they boil higher than alcohols of similar mass. C1–C4 acids are miscible with water; solubility falls with chain length. Lower acids have sharp smells; higher ones are waxy solids.

visual.alt: Table of boiling points of compounds of similar mass

slides.narration: In the carboxyl group, the carbon is sp two hybridised and the hydroxyl lone pair is shared with the carbonyl group, which makes the carbonyl less reactive than in aldehydes. Two acid molecules link through two hydrogen bonds to form a dimer, which behaves like a much larger molecule. That is why ethanoic acid boils higher than propan-one-ol of the same mass.

slides.heading: Quick check: names and properties
slides.body_md: Name an acid or explain its boiling point.
slides.narration: Quick check. Diacids end in dioic acid; dimers explain high boiling points.

slides.heading: Preparation of aliphatic acids
slides.body_md: **Oxidation** of 1° alcohols and aldehydes (KMnO₄ or K₂Cr₂O₇ in acid). **Hydrolysis of nitriles** (H₃O⁺ or OH⁻, heat) — one carbon more than the alkyl halide. **Grignard reagent + CO₂** (dry ice), then H₃O⁺ — one carbon more. Also hydrolysis of esters, amides and acid chlorides.

visual.alt: Table of preparations of aliphatic acids

slides.narration: Strong oxidation of primary alcohols and aldehydes gives carboxylic acids. Hydrolysing a nitrile with acid or alkali converts the CN group into COOH; since the nitrile was made from an alkyl halide and cyanide, the acid has one more carbon than the halide. Grignard reagents add to carbon dioxide, and acid work-up gives an acid, again with one extra carbon.

slides.heading: Preparation of aromatic acids
slides.body_md: **Oxidation of alkylbenzenes** with hot alkaline KMnO₄ (then acid): any alkyl side chain with a benzylic H → –COOH. Also from **benzonitrile** (hydrolysis), **phenylmagnesium bromide + CO₂**, and oxidation of benzaldehyde or benzyl alcohol.

visual.alt: Table of preparations of aromatic acids

slides.narration: For aromatic acids, hot alkaline potassium permanganate oxidises any alkyl side chain, whatever its length, down to a single carboxyl group on the ring, so toluene and ethylbenzene both give benzoic acid. Benzoic acid can also be made by hydrolysing benzonitrile or by adding carbon dioxide to phenylmagnesium bromide. Para-xylene gives terephthalic acid, used to make polyester.

slides.heading: Worked example: planning a synthesis
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** (a) Prepare butanoic acid from 1-bromopropane by two routes. (b) Prepare 4-methylbenzoic acid from 4-bromotoluene.

**(a)** Route 1: KCN (ethanol) → butanenitrile; H₃O⁺, heat → butanoic acid. Route 2: Mg, dry ether → $\ce{CH3CH2CH2MgBr}$; CO₂, then H₃O⁺ → butanoic acid.

**(b)** Mg, dry ether → 4-methylphenylmagnesium bromide; CO₂, then H₃O⁺ → 4-methylbenzoic acid. (KMnO₄ is not used: it would oxidise the methyl group too.)

visual.alt: Flow of two routes from 1-bromopropane to butanoic acid

slides.narration: Both the nitrile and the Grignard routes add one carbon, so the three-carbon bromide gives the four-carbon acid. For four-methylbenzoic acid, the Grignard route converts only the bromine position into a carboxyl group and leaves the methyl group alone; permanganate would oxidise the methyl group as well, giving a diacid.

slides.heading: Quick check: preparation
slides.body_md: Choose a route to a given carboxylic acid.
slides.narration: Quick check. Nitrile and Grignard routes add one carbon; permanganate cuts any side chain down to COOH.

slides.heading: Why carboxylic acids are acidic
slides.body_md: $\ce{RCOOH + H2O <=> RCOO- + H3O+}$. The **carboxylate ion** is stabilised by **two equivalent resonance structures**: the charge is shared equally by two **oxygen** atoms (both C–O bonds 127 pm). Carboxylic acids (pKa ≈ 4–5) are stronger than phenols (≈ 10) and alcohols (≈ 16), and decompose NaHCO₃.

slides.narration: When a carboxylic acid loses a proton, the negative charge on the carboxylate ion is shared equally between two electronegative oxygen atoms, through two identical resonance structures; both carbon to oxygen bonds become the same length. This stabilisation is greater than in the phenoxide ion, where the charge spreads onto less electronegative carbon atoms. So carboxylic acids are stronger than phenols and release carbon dioxide from hydrogencarbonates.

slides.heading: Substituent effects in aliphatic acids
slides.body_md: **Electron-withdrawing** groups (−I: –F, –Cl, –NO₂, –CN) stabilise the carboxylate → **stronger acid**. Effect grows with the **number** and **electronegativity** of the groups and falls with **distance** from –COOH. **Electron-releasing** alkyl groups (+I) → weaker acid.

visual.alt: Table of pKa values of aliphatic acids

slides.narration: Electron-withdrawing groups pull electron density away from the carboxylate and stabilise it, so the acid is stronger. Three chlorines make trichloroethanoic acid almost as strong as a mineral acid. Fluorine, being more electronegative, has a larger effect than chlorine. Alkyl groups push electrons in and make acids weaker, which is why methanoic acid, with none, is stronger than ethanoic acid.

slides.heading: Substituent effects in aromatic acids
slides.body_md: Benzoic acid (pKa 4.19) is stronger than ethanoic acid. Electron-withdrawing groups (–NO₂, –Cl) **increase** acidity; electron-donating groups (–CH₃, –OCH₃, –OH at para by +R) **decrease** it. Most **ortho**-substituted benzoic acids are stronger than benzoic acid whatever the group (**ortho effect**).

visual.alt: Table of pKa values of substituted benzoic acids

slides.narration: The same ideas apply to benzoic acids. A nitro group withdraws electrons and makes four-nitrobenzoic acid stronger. Methyl and methoxy groups release electrons, especially at the para position, and make the acid weaker. Groups at the ortho position usually make the acid stronger, whatever their electronic nature; this is called the ortho effect and is partly due to the group twisting the carboxyl group out of the plane of the ring.

slides.heading: Worked example: effect of distance
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Arrange in decreasing acid strength and explain: butanoic acid, 2-chlorobutanoic acid, 3-chlorobutanoic acid, 4-chlorobutanoic acid. (pKa: 4.82, 2.86, 4.05, 4.52)

**Step 1.** Cl withdraws electrons (−I), stabilising the carboxylate.

**Step 2.** The −I effect weakens rapidly with the number of bonds between Cl and –COOH.

**Order:** 2-chloro (2.86) > 3-chloro (4.05) > 4-chloro (4.52) > butanoic acid (4.82).

visual.alt: Table showing the effect of distance on acid strength

slides.narration: All three chloro acids are stronger than butanoic acid, because chlorine withdraws electrons and stabilises the carboxylate. But the inductive effect fades quickly with distance. With chlorine on the carbon next to the carboxyl group, the effect is large; one carbon further away, much smaller; two carbons away, only slight.

slides.heading: Quick check: acid strength
slides.body_md: Pick the strongest or weakest acid from a set.
slides.narration: Quick check. Count and locate the electron-withdrawing groups; alkyl groups weaken acids.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 1
bullets: Names: -oic acid; diacids -dioic acid (oxalic, succinic, adipic, phthalic).
H-bonded dimers → high b.p.; C1–C4 miscible with water.
Preparation: oxidation of 1° alcohols/aldehydes; nitrile hydrolysis; RMgX + CO₂; alkylbenzene + KMnO₄ → benzoic acid.
Acidity from carboxylate resonance (two equivalent O); stronger than phenols; decompose NaHCO₃.
−I groups increase acidity (more, closer, more electronegative); +I/+R groups decrease it; ortho effect.

visual.alt: Summary table of pKa values

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part 1. Carboxylic acids are named with the ending oic acid. Hydrogen-bonded dimers give them high boiling points. They are made by oxidation, by hydrolysing nitriles and from Grignard reagents and carbon dioxide; side chains on benzene rings are oxidised to carboxyl groups. Resonance in the carboxylate ion makes them acidic, and substituents raise or lower their strength.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 1
bullets: In acidity questions, name the effect (−I, +I, −R, +R) and its direction.
Nitrile and Grignard routes add one carbon; say so in synthesis answers.
Draw both resonance structures of the carboxylate ion.

rows: KMnO₄ on propylbenzene gives propanoic acid

visual.alt: Table of three common slips in Part 1 and fixes

slides.narration: Some tips. In acid-strength questions, name each electronic effect and say whether it increases or decreases acidity. Remember that the inductive effect weakens with distance. Point out that nitrile and Grignard routes add a carbon. And draw both resonance structures of the carboxylate ion when explaining acidity.

decks.title: Carboxylic Acids — Part 2: Reactions, tests and uses
goals: Write reactions with active metals, alkalis, carbonates and hydrogencarbonates
Write equations for forming acid chlorides, anhydrides, esters and amides
Write decarboxylation, Kolbe electrolysis and HVZ reactions; predict ring substitution of benzoic acid
Describe tests for and uses of formic, acetic and benzoic acids

slides.heading: Reactions of carboxylic acids
slides.body_md: Part 2 — acidic reactions, acid derivatives, losing CO₂, α-halogenation, ring substitution, tests and uses.

nodes.label: Acid reactions: Na, NaOH, Na₂CO₃, NaHCO₃

visual.alt: Flow of the reactions in Part 2

slides.narration: Carboxylic acids show typical acid reactions with metals, alkalis and carbonates. Replacing their hydroxyl group gives a family of derivatives: acid chlorides, anhydrides, esters and amides. Their salts can lose carbon dioxide, and their alpha hydrogens can be replaced by halogens. Finally we meet simple tests for formic, acetic and benzoic acids, and their uses.

slides.heading: Reactions as acids
slides.body_md: Carboxylic acids react with **active metals** (H₂), **alkalis** (salt + water), **carbonates** and **hydrogencarbonates** (CO₂ effervescence — a test that distinguishes them from phenols).

visual.alt: Table of acidic reactions

slides.narration: Carboxylic acids react with sodium to give hydrogen, and with alkalis to give salts and water. Unlike phenols, they are strong enough to decompose carbonates and hydrogencarbonates, releasing carbon dioxide with brisk effervescence. That makes sodium hydrogencarbonate a quick test to tell a carboxylic acid from a phenol.

slides.heading: Acid derivatives
slides.body_md: Replacing –OH gives derivatives. **Acid chlorides:** PCl₅, PCl₃ or SOCl₂. **Anhydrides:** heat with P₂O₅ (dehydration of two molecules). **Esters:** alcohol + conc. H₂SO₄ (reversible). **Amides:** NH₃ gives the ammonium salt, which loses water on heating.

visual.alt: Table of acid derivatives

slides.narration: Phosphorus chlorides and thionyl chloride convert carboxylic acids into acid chlorides, which are very reactive. Heating with phosphorus pentoxide removes water from two molecules to form an anhydride. Alcohols with concentrated sulphuric acid give esters. With ammonia, an ammonium salt forms first, which loses water on strong heating to give an amide.

slides.heading: Worked example: derivatives of benzoic acid
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Give the product of benzoic acid with (a) SOCl₂; (b) ethanol + conc. H₂SO₄; (c) NH₃, then strong heating; (d) PCl₅.

**(a)** Benzoyl chloride, $\ce{C6H5COCl}$ (+ SO₂ + HCl).

**(b)** Ethyl benzoate, $\ce{C6H5COOC2H5}$.

**(c)** Benzamide, $\ce{C6H5CONH2}$ (via ammonium benzoate).

**(d)** Benzoyl chloride (+ POCl₃ + HCl).

visual.alt: Table of benzoic acid derivatives

slides.narration: Benzoic acid forms the same derivatives as aliphatic acids. Thionyl chloride or phosphorus pentachloride gives benzoyl chloride. Ethanol with a little concentrated sulphuric acid gives ethyl benzoate, a pleasant-smelling ester. Ammonia gives ammonium benzoate, which on strong heating loses water to form benzamide.

slides.heading: Quick check: acid and derivative reactions
slides.body_md: Predict the product of a carboxylic acid with a given reagent.
slides.narration: Quick check. Sodium hydrogencarbonate gives carbon dioxide; chlorinating agents give acid chlorides.

slides.heading: Decarboxylation and Kolbe electrolysis
slides.body_md: **Chemical decarboxylation:** sodium salt + **soda lime** (NaOH + CaO), heat → alkane with **one carbon fewer**. **Kolbe electrolysis:** electrolysis of an aqueous sodium/potassium salt; at the anode, carboxylate radicals lose CO₂ and **couple**: alkane with **2(n − 1)** carbons.

visual.alt: Table of decarboxylation products

slides.narration: Heating the sodium salt of an acid with soda lime removes the carboxyl group as carbonate, leaving an alkane with one carbon fewer: sodium propanoate gives ethane. In Kolbe electrolysis, carboxylate ions lose an electron and carbon dioxide at the anode, and the alkyl radicals join in pairs, so sodium ethanoate gives ethane and sodium propanoate gives butane. Hydrogen is released at the cathode.

slides.heading: Hell–Volhard–Zelinsky reaction
slides.body_md: Acids with **α-hydrogen** react with Cl₂ or Br₂ in the presence of a little **red phosphorus**: α-H is replaced by halogen, giving **α-halo acids**; further halogenation gives di- and tri-halo acids.

visual.alt: Table of HVZ reactions

slides.narration: In the Hell–Volhard–Zelinsky reaction, chlorine or bromine with a little red phosphorus replaces a hydrogen on the carbon next to the carboxyl group. Propanoic acid gives two-bromopropanoic acid, and with excess chlorine ethanoic acid can be converted all the way to trichloroethanoic acid. Benzoic acid has no alpha hydrogen, so it does not react this way.

slides.heading: Ring substitution in benzoic acid
slides.body_md: –COOH withdraws electrons (−I, −R): **deactivating** and **meta directing**. Nitration → 3-nitrobenzoic acid; bromination (Br₂/FeBr₃) → 3-bromobenzoic acid. Benzoic acid does **not** undergo Friedel–Crafts reactions (deactivated ring; –COOH complexes AlCl₃).

visual.alt: Table of ring substitution of benzoic acid

slides.narration: The carboxyl group pulls electrons out of the ring, so benzoic acid reacts more slowly than benzene in electrophilic substitution, and the new group goes to the meta position. Nitration gives three-nitrobenzoic acid and bromination three-bromobenzoic acid. Friedel–Crafts reactions fail, because the ring is deactivated and the carboxyl group ties up the aluminium chloride catalyst.

slides.heading: Worked example: losing and gaining groups
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Name the product: (a) sodium butanoate + soda lime, heat; (b) Kolbe electrolysis of potassium propanoate; (c) butanoic acid + Br₂/red P; (d) benzoic acid + conc. HNO₃/H₂SO₄.

**(a)** Propane. **(b)** Butane (2 × ethyl).

**(c)** 2-Bromobutanoic acid. **(d)** 3-Nitrobenzoic acid.

visual.alt: Table of products

slides.narration: Soda lime removes the carboxyl carbon, so sodium butanoate gives propane. In Kolbe electrolysis of propanoate, each ion loses carbon dioxide to give an ethyl radical, and two ethyl radicals join to form butane. Bromine with red phosphorus substitutes the alpha position, giving two-bromobutanoic acid. Nitration of benzoic acid goes meta.

slides.heading: Quick check: decarboxylation and HVZ
slides.body_md: Predict the product of soda-lime heating, Kolbe electrolysis or the HVZ reaction.
slides.narration: Quick check. Soda lime: one carbon fewer. Kolbe: two alkyl groups joined. HVZ: halogen at the alpha carbon.

slides.heading: Tests for formic, acetic and benzoic acids
slides.body_md: All three effervesce with NaHCO₃. **Formic acid** (H–COOH has an aldehyde-like H): reduces **Tollens’** reagent (silver mirror), **Fehling’s** (red ppt) and HgCl₂ (white ppt → grey). **Acetic acid:** neutral FeCl₃ → **deep red** colour (brown-red ppt on boiling); ester smell with ethanol/H₂SO₄. **Benzoic acid:** neutral FeCl₃ → **buff (pale brown) precipitate**; sublimes on heating.

visual.alt: Table of tests for formic, acetic and benzoic acids

slides.narration: All carboxylic acids fizz with sodium hydrogencarbonate. Formic acid is special: its hydrogen on the carboxyl carbon behaves like that of an aldehyde, so it reduces Tollens’ reagent, Fehling’s solution and mercury two chloride. With neutral iron three chloride, acetate gives a deep red colour, while benzoate gives a buff precipitate. These tests identify the three acids.

slides.heading: Uses
slides.body_md: Important uses of the three acids and related compounds.

rows: Coagulating rubber latex; dyeing and tanning; antiseptic; preserving fruit juice
Vinegar; solvent; making cellulose acetate, acetic anhydride, esters
Sodium benzoate food preservative; medicines (urinary antiseptic); making dyes

visual.alt: Table of uses of carboxylic acids

slides.narration: Formic acid is used to coagulate rubber latex and in dyeing and tanning. Acetic acid is vinegar, and is used to make cellulose acetate, acetic anhydride and esters. Benzoic acid, as sodium benzoate, preserves pickles and sauces. Hexanedioic acid is used to make nylon, and terephthalic acid to make polyester fibres.

slides.heading: Quick check: tests
slides.body_md: Choose the test that distinguishes formic, acetic or benzoic acid.
slides.narration: Quick check. Formic acid reduces Tollens’ reagent; neutral iron three chloride gives different results with acetate and benzoate.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 2
bullets: Na → H₂; NaOH → salt; Na₂CO₃/NaHCO₃ → CO₂ (not phenols).
Derivatives: RCOCl (PCl₅, PCl₃, SOCl₂); (RCO)₂O (P₂O₅); RCOOR′ (R′OH, H⁺); RCONH₂ (NH₃, heat).
Soda lime: alkane with one C fewer; Kolbe electrolysis: R–R; HVZ: α-halo acid (X₂, red P).
Benzoic acid: meta substitution; no Friedel–Crafts.
Formic acid reduces Tollens’/Fehling’s/HgCl₂; acetate + FeCl₃ red; benzoate + FeCl₃ buff ppt.

visual.alt: Summary table of reactions

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part 2. Carboxylic acids react as acids with metals, alkalis and carbonates. Their hydroxyl group can be replaced to give acid chlorides, anhydrides, esters and amides. Their salts lose carbon dioxide with soda lime or on electrolysis, and their alpha hydrogens can be halogenated. Benzoic acid is substituted at the meta position, and simple tests distinguish formic, acetic and benzoic acids.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 2
bullets: For Kolbe electrolysis, double the alkyl group after removing CO₂.
HVZ needs α-H and red phosphorus.
Formic acid is the only common acid that reduces Tollens’ reagent.
Use NaHCO₃ to distinguish acids from phenols.

visual.alt: Table of three common slips in Part 2 and fixes

slides.narration: Final tips. In Kolbe electrolysis, remove carbon dioxide and join two alkyl groups. Remember that the HVZ reaction needs an alpha hydrogen and red phosphorus. Formic acid is unique in reducing Tollens’ reagent. And sodium hydrogencarbonate distinguishes carboxylic acids from phenols.

notes.title: Carboxylic Acids — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Classification, names and physical properties
sections.body_md:
Mono- (CₙH₂ₙ₊₁COOH) and dicarboxylic acids. IUPAC **-oic acid**: 2-methylpropanoic acid; diacids **-dioic acid**: ethanedioic (oxalic), propanedioic (malonic), butanedioic (succinic), hexanedioic (adipic); benzene-1,2-dicarboxylic (phthalic).

Carboxyl C sp²; **H-bonded cyclic dimers** → b.p. higher than alcohols of similar mass (ethanoic 391 K vs propan-1-ol 370 K). C1–C4 miscible with water.

key_terms.definition_md: Two acid molecules held by two hydrogen bonds.

visual.alt: Table of names

sections.heading: 2. Preparation
sections.body_md:
- Oxidation of 1° alcohols and aldehydes (K₂Cr₂O₇/H⁺, KMnO₄).
- Alkylbenzenes + hot alkaline KMnO₄, then H⁺ → benzoic acid (any side chain).
- Nitrile hydrolysis: $\ce{RCN + 2H2O + HCl -> RCOOH + NH4Cl}$ (one C more than RX).
- Grignard: $\ce{RMgX + CO2 -> RCOOMgX}$, then H₃O⁺ (one C more).

key_terms.definition_md: Solid CO₂, used with Grignard reagents to make carboxylic acids.

visual.alt: Table of preparations

sections.heading: 3. Acidity
sections.body_md:
Carboxylate stabilised by **two equivalent resonance structures** (charge on two O; C–O both 127 pm) → pKa 4–5; stronger than phenols (10) and alcohols (16); decompose NaHCO₃.

**Substituents:** −I groups (F > Cl > Br; more groups; nearer –COOH) increase acidity: CCl₃COOH 0.65, CHCl₂COOH 1.26, FCH₂COOH 2.66, ClCH₂COOH 2.86; 2-, 3-, 4-chlorobutanoic 2.86, 4.05, 4.52. +I alkyl groups decrease: HCOOH 3.75 > CH₃COOH 4.76 > CH₃CH₂COOH 4.88.

**Benzoic acids:** 4-NO₂ 3.41, 4-Cl 3.98, H 4.19, 4-CH₃ 4.37, 4-OCH₃ 4.47; ortho-substituted acids usually stronger (ortho effect).

key_terms.definition_md: Electron withdrawal (−I) or release (+I) through σ bonds; weakens with distance.
Most ortho-substituted benzoic acids are stronger than benzoic acid regardless of the substituent.

sections.heading: 4. Acid reactions and derivatives
sections.body_md:
Na → H₂; NaOH → salt + H₂O; Na₂CO₃/NaHCO₃ → CO₂ (phenols do not).

**Derivatives:** PCl₅ ($\ce{RCOOH + PCl5 -> RCOCl + POCl3 + HCl}$), PCl₃ (+ H₃PO₃), SOCl₂ (+ SO₂ + HCl) → acid chlorides; P₂O₅/heat → anhydrides; R′OH + conc. H₂SO₄ → esters (reversible); NH₃ → RCOONH₄ → (heat) RCONH₂.

key_terms.definition_md: A compound in which the –OH of –COOH is replaced: acid chloride, anhydride, ester, amide.

visual.alt: Table of derivatives

sections.heading: 5. Decarboxylation, Kolbe electrolysis, HVZ and ring substitution
sections.body_md: **Soda lime** (NaOH + CaO): $\ce{RCOONa + NaOH -> RH + Na2CO3}$ (one C fewer). **Kolbe electrolysis:** $\ce{2RCOO- -> R-R + 2CO2 + 2e-}$ at the anode (R–R). **HVZ:** α-H + X₂ (red P) → α-halo acid; excess Cl₂ → CCl₃COOH. **Benzoic acid:** –COOH deactivating, meta directing (3-nitro-, 3-bromobenzoic acid); no Friedel–Crafts.

key_terms.definition_md: Removal of CO₂ from a carboxylic acid or its salt.
α-Halogenation of carboxylic acids with X₂ and red phosphorus.

visual.alt: Table of decarboxylation products

sections.heading: 6. Tests and uses
sections.body_md:
All three effervesce with NaHCO₃. **Formic acid:** reduces Tollens’ (silver mirror), Fehling’s (red ppt), HgCl₂ (white Hg₂Cl₂ → grey). **Acetic acid:** neutral FeCl₃ → deep red colour (brown-red ppt on boiling); fruity ester with ethanol/H₂SO₄. **Benzoic acid:** neutral FeCl₃ → buff precipitate; sublimes.

**Uses:** formic — rubber coagulation, dyeing, tanning; acetic — vinegar, cellulose acetate, esters, solvent; benzoic — sodium benzoate preservative, medicines, dyes; adipic — nylon-6,6; terephthalic — polyester.

key_terms.definition_md: Distinguishes ethanoate (red colour) from benzoate (buff precipitate).

visual.alt: Table of tests

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Ranking CH₃COOH above HCOOH in acid strength.
- Forgetting that −I effects fade with distance.
- Kolbe electrolysis of ethanoate giving methane (it gives ethane).
- Applying HVZ to benzoic acid (no α-H).

**How marks are usually awarded**
- Acid strength (2–3 marks): correct order plus named electronic effects.
- Preparations (1 mark each): reagent, condition and product; mention carbon count.
- Tests (1–2 marks): reagent and result for each acid.

questions.stem_md: Draw (describe) the hydrogen-bonded dimer of ethanoic acid and use it to explain why ethanoic acid boils higher than propan-1-ol.

answer.model_answer_md: Two CH₃COOH molecules are joined by two O–H···O=C hydrogen bonds into an eight-membered ring (dimer), effectively doubling the molar mass. The dimer persists even in the vapour, so more energy is needed to boil the acid than propan-1-ol, whose molecules form single, chain-like hydrogen bonds.

questions.stem_md: $0.25\ \text{mol}$ of phenylmagnesium bromide reacts completely with excess dry ice, and the product is acidified. What mass of benzoic acid ($M = 122$) is formed?
Write equations for preparing benzoic acid from (a) benzonitrile and (b) phenylmagnesium bromide.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) $\ce{C6H5CN + 2H2O + HCl -> C6H5COOH + NH4Cl}$. (b) $\ce{C6H5MgBr + CO2 -> C6H5COOMgBr}$; then $\ce{C6H5COOMgBr + H2O ->[H+] C6H5COOH + Mg(OH)Br}$.

questions.stem_md: Show how butanoic acid can be obtained from (a) butan-1-ol, (b) 1-bromopropane via a nitrile and (c) 1-bromopropane via a Grignard reagent.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) K₂Cr₂O₇/H₂SO₄, reflux (oxidation). (b) KCN in ethanol → butanenitrile; then hot dilute acid (hydrolysis). (c) Mg in dry ether → propylmagnesium bromide; dry ice, then dilute acid.

questions.stem_md: (a) Why is KMnO₄ unsuitable for converting 4-bromotoluene into 4-methylbenzoic acid? (b) Suggest a suitable route. (c) What would KMnO₄ give?

answer.model_answer_md: (a) KMnO₄ oxidises the methyl side chain to –COOH. (b) Mg in dry ether to form the Grignard reagent at the C–Br position, then CO₂ and dilute acid: 4-methylbenzoic acid. (c) 4-Bromobenzoic acid.

questions.solution_md: Side chain oxidised; Grignard route; 4-bromobenzoic acid.

questions.stem_md: Which is the strongest acid: CH₃COOH, ClCH₂COOH, Cl₂CHCOOH or Cl₃CCOOH?
questions.solution_md: Three −I chlorines stabilise the carboxylate most (pKa 0.65) — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Which chlorobutanoic acid is the strongest acid?
questions.solution_md: The −I effect is greatest when Cl is nearest to –COOH — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Which substituted benzoic acid is the weakest acid?

**Reason (R):** Fluorine is more electronegative than chlorine and has a stronger −I effect.

Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Benzoic acid releases CO₂ from aqueous NaHCO₃, but phenol does not.

**Reason (R):** Benzoic acid contains a benzene ring.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, but A is due to the greater stability of the carboxylate (charge on two O atoms), not to the ring, which phenol also has — option (b).

questions.stem_md: True or false? 2-Methylbenzoic acid is a stronger acid than benzoic acid, although methyl is an electron-releasing group.
The pKa of chloroethanoic acid is 2.86 and that of ethanoic acid is 4.76. By what factor is the $K_\text{a}$ of chloroethanoic acid larger? Give your answer to the nearest whole number.
Using resonance, explain why ethanoic acid (pKa 4.76) is a much stronger acid than ethanol (pKa about 16).

answer.model_answer_md: In the ethanoate ion the negative charge is delocalised equally over two oxygen atoms (two equivalent resonance structures), stabilising the ion. In the ethoxide ion the charge is localised on one oxygen and is further destabilised by the +I effect of the ethyl group. The more stable the anion, the stronger the acid.

questions.stem_md: Arrange benzoic acid, 4-nitrobenzoic acid and 4-methylbenzoic acid in increasing acid strength and explain.

answer.model_answer_md: 4-Methylbenzoic < benzoic < 4-nitrobenzoic. –CH₃ releases electrons (+I, hyperconjugation), destabilising the carboxylate; –NO₂ withdraws electrons (−I, −R), stabilising it.

questions.stem_md: Arrange the following in order of increasing acid strength and explain: CH₃CH₂COOH, CH₃CHClCOOH, ClCH₂CH₂COOH, CH₃CCl₂COOH.

answer.model_answer_md: CH₃CH₂COOH < ClCH₂CH₂COOH < CH₃CHClCOOH < CH₃CCl₂COOH. Chlorine’s −I effect stabilises the carboxylate; it is weaker when Cl is on the β-carbon (farther) than on the α-carbon, and two α-chlorines have a greater effect than one. Propanoic acid has no electron-withdrawing group.

questions.solution_md: Order with number and distance reasoning.

questions.stem_md: Explain the effect on the acid strength of benzoic acid of (a) a nitro group at the para position, (b) a methoxy group at the para position and (c) a methyl group at the ortho position.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Increases acidity: –NO₂ withdraws electrons by −I and −R, stabilising the carboxylate. (b) Decreases acidity: –OCH₃ releases electrons by +R (outweighing −I) at the para position. (c) Increases acidity (ortho effect): the ortho group forces –COOH out of the ring plane, reducing the ring’s electron donation to it, so the acid is stronger.

questions.stem_md: Sodium butanoate is heated with soda lime. The gas evolved is:

questions.stem_md: Soda lime, used for decarboxylating sodium salts of acids, is a mixture of sodium hydroxide and ___.

answer.model_answer_md: Carboxylic acids with α-hydrogen react with Cl₂ or Br₂ in the presence of a little red phosphorus to give α-halo acids. $\ce{CH3CH2COOH + Br2 ->[red P] CH3CHBrCOOH + HBr}$ (2-bromopropanoic acid).

questions.stem_md: Explain what happens at the anode during Kolbe electrolysis of aqueous sodium propanoate, and name the hydrocarbon formed.

answer.model_answer_md: Propanoate ions lose an electron at the anode to give carboxyl radicals CH₃CH₂COO•, which lose CO₂ to give ethyl radicals; two ethyl radicals combine to form butane, CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₃. (H₂ and NaOH form at the cathode.)

questions.stem_md: Name the product when (a) sodium benzoate is heated with soda lime, (b) ethanoic acid is treated with excess chlorine and red phosphorus and (c) benzoic acid is nitrated.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Benzene. (b) Trichloroethanoic acid, CCl₃COOH (HVZ, repeated). (c) 3-Nitrobenzoic acid.

questions.stem_md: Which of methanoic, ethanoic and benzoic acid gives a silver mirror with Tollens’ reagent?
questions.solution_md: H–COOH contains an aldehyde-like H — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A neutral solution of a sodium salt gives a buff (pale brown) precipitate with neutral iron(III) chloride. The salt is most likely:
questions.solution_md: Benzoate gives buff iron(III) benzoate; ethanoate gives a deep red colour — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Methanoic acid is warmed with mercury(II) chloride solution. The observation is:

The sodium salt of benzoic acid, used as a food preservative, is sodium ___.
True or false? A neutral solution of sodium ethanoate gives a deep red colour with neutral iron(III) chloride.
questions.solution_md: True; on boiling a brown-red precipitate forms.

questions.stem_md: $0.46\ \text{g}$ of methanoic acid ($M = 46$) reduces excess Tollens’ reagent: $\ce{HCOOH + 2[Ag(NH3)2]+ + 2OH- -> 2Ag + CO2 + 2H2O + 4NH3}$. What mass of silver ($M = 108$) is deposited?
Give one chemical test, with observations, to distinguish (a) methanoic acid from ethanoic acid and (b) ethanoic acid from benzoic acid.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Tollens’ reagent (or Fehling’s): methanoic acid gives a silver mirror (or red precipitate); ethanoic acid does not. (b) Neutralise and add neutral FeCl₃: ethanoate gives a deep red colour; benzoate gives a buff precipitate.

questions.stem_md: Give one important use each of (a) methanoic acid, (b) ethanoic acid and (c) benzoic acid or its sodium salt.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Coagulating rubber latex (or dyeing, tanning, preserving fruit). (b) Vinegar; making cellulose acetate, acetic anhydride or esters; solvent. (c) Sodium benzoate as a food preservative (or medicines, dyes).

questions.stem_md: Methanoic acid shows some reactions of aldehydes. (a) Explain why, using its structure. (b) Write the equation for its reaction with HgCl₂. (c) Name one other reagent it reduces.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) H–COOH: the carboxyl carbon carries a hydrogen, as in an aldehyde (H–C=O), so it is easily oxidised to CO₂. (b) $\ce{HCOOH + 2HgCl2 -> Hg2Cl2 + CO2 + 2HCl}$. (c) Tollens’ reagent (silver mirror) or Fehling’s solution (red Cu₂O).

questions.stem_md:
(a) Write equations to prepare propanoic acid from (i) propan-1-ol, (ii) propanenitrile and (iii) ethylmagnesium bromide. [3]

(b) Explain, using hydrogen-bonded dimers, why propanoic acid boils higher than butan-1-ol of similar mass. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) (i) $\ce{CH3CH2CH2OH ->[K2Cr2O7/H2SO4][reflux] CH3CH2COOH}$ (skeletal; oxidation). (ii) $\ce{CH3CH2CN + 2H2O + HCl -> CH3CH2COOH + NH4Cl}$. (iii) $\ce{CH3CH2MgBr + CO2 -> CH3CH2COOMgBr}$, then dilute acid gives $\ce{CH3CH2COOH}$.

(b) Two propanoic acid molecules are held together by two hydrogen bonds in a cyclic dimer, which behaves as a larger molecule and persists in the vapour; butan-1-ol forms only single chain hydrogen bonds, so less energy is needed to boil it.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Explain why carboxylic acids are stronger acids than phenols. [1½]

(b) Arrange in increasing acid strength and explain: CH₃COOH, ClCH₂COOH, FCH₂COOH, Cl₂CHCOOH. [2]

(c) Explain why 4-nitrobenzoic acid is stronger, and 4-methylbenzoic acid weaker, than benzoic acid. [1½]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) In the carboxylate ion the negative charge is shared equally by two electronegative oxygen atoms (equivalent resonance structures); in the phenoxide ion it is delocalised onto less electronegative ring carbons, and the structures are not equivalent. So the carboxylate is more stable.

(b) CH₃COOH < ClCH₂COOH < FCH₂COOH < Cl₂CHCOOH. −I groups stabilise the carboxylate; F is more electronegative than Cl; two Cl atoms exert a greater −I effect than one.

(c) –NO₂ withdraws electrons (−I, −R), stabilising the anion; –CH₃ releases electrons (+I, hyperconjugation), destabilising it.

questions.solution_md: Carboxylate vs phenoxide; −I order; benzoic substituents.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Write equations for the formation of (i) ethanoyl chloride with SOCl₂, (ii) ethanoic anhydride and (iii) ethanamide from ethanoic acid. [3]

(b) Write equations for (i) decarboxylation of sodium ethanoate with soda lime and (ii) Kolbe electrolysis of sodium ethanoate. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) (i) $\ce{CH3COOH + SOCl2 -> CH3COCl + SO2 + HCl}$. (ii) $\ce{2CH3COOH ->[P2O5][\Delta] (CH3CO)2O + H2O}$. (iii) $\ce{CH3COOH + NH3 -> CH3COONH4}$; $\ce{CH3COONH4 ->[\Delta] CH3CONH2 + H2O}$.

(b) (i) $\ce{CH3COONa + NaOH ->[CaO][\Delta] CH4 + Na2CO3}$. (ii) $\ce{2CH3COONa + 2H2O -> CH3CH3 + 2CO2 + 2NaOH + H2}$.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Describe the HVZ reaction with an equation for propanoic acid. [1½]

(b) Explain why the –COOH group is meta directing, and give the product of nitrating benzoic acid. [2]

(c) How would you distinguish methanoic, ethanoic and benzoic acids by chemical tests? [1½]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Acids with α-H react with Cl₂/Br₂ and a little red P, replacing α-H by halogen: $\ce{CH3CH2COOH + Br2 ->[red P] CH3CHBrCOOH + HBr}$.

(b) –COOH withdraws electrons (−I, −R); for ortho/para attack one resonance form of the σ-complex puts + on the carbon bearing –COOH (destabilised), so meta attack is favoured. Product: 3-nitrobenzoic acid.

(c) Methanoic acid gives a silver mirror with Tollens’ reagent (others do not). Neutral FeCl₃ with the neutralised acids: ethanoate deep red colour; benzoate buff precipitate.

questions.stem_md:
Compound A, C₂H₄O₂, dissolves in NaHCO₃ with effervescence and gives a deep red colour with neutral FeCl₃ after neutralisation. A reacts with Cl₂/red P to give B, and with ethanol/H₂SO₄ to give a fruity-smelling C. The sodium salt of A, heated with soda lime, gives a gas D.

(a) Identify A, B, C and D. [4]

(b) Write the equation for the formation of C. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) A: ethanoic acid, CH₃COOH. B: chloroethanoic acid, ClCH₂COOH. C: ethyl ethanoate, CH₃COOC₂H₅. D: methane, CH₄.

(b) $\ce{CH3COOH + C2H5OH <=>[H+] CH3COOC2H5 + H2O}$.

questions.solution_md: Ethanoic acid; chloroethanoic acid; ethyl ethanoate; methane.
